title: How Cleta Mitchell Turned Trump’s “Big Lie” Into a Movement
author: Doug Bock Clark
content:
In July, not long before President Donald Trump delivered a [primetime
address](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iIlqG0untYM) questioning the
legitimacy of American elections, the pioneering conservative election lawyer
Cleta Mitchell and about two dozen of her associates logged onto a private
video briefing with the White House.

Mitchell, who holds no formal position in the Trump administration, had been
pivotal to Trump’s bid to challenge his loss in 2020, spearheading efforts to
prove his claims of fraud and reverse his defeat in court.

After Joe Biden took office, when others abandoned the fight or scoffed as
Trump clung to conspiracy theories, Mitchell doubled down, founding a
grassroots organization devoted to rewriting election laws and rules to be
more restrictive. Members of her group, the Election Integrity Network, were
named to vital election-related positions in swing states and, later, in the
second Trump administration.

The pre-speech briefing was an acknowledgment of just how consequential
Mitchell and her organization had become. The White House had held similar
sessions for key political players, such as governors, members of Congress and
major press outlets.

* * *

### Help Us Report on Key Election Issues

ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what
isn’t. We’re monitoring **voter suppression** and interference, **election
observers** and**** poll watchers, **extremism** tied to the election,
and**ICE activity** at the polls. Have you seen something?

[Send Us a Tip](https://www.propublica.org/tips/)

* * *

At the appointed time, the screen filled with the faces of EIN leaders and
supporters, some sitting in front of digital backgrounds with the group’s logo
on them. Mitchell shushed those who’d forgotten to mute and introduced John
Solomon, an ally of hers who was helping prepare the speech.

Mitchell and her network hardly needed the run-through, though: Much of the
speech was a compendium of allegations and conspiracy theories they had
originated or spread.

Her lieutenants were thrilled to hear that the president would assert there
were more than 275,000 noncitizens on state voter rolls — a [since-debunked
claim](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/us/politics/nevada-voters-homeland-
security-trump.html) based on work led by one of her proteges, who occupied a
top post at the Department of Homeland Security.

The speech would end with an exhortation for Congress to pass the SAVE America
Act, a bill requiring voters to provide documentary proof of citizenship to
register, which Mitchell had helped draft.

To Seth Keshel, an EIN adviser on the call, none of it was surprising —
Mitchell was in and out of the White House all the time. He’d joined her for
one such meeting.

“She’s got an open door with the president,” he said.

![A portrait of a woman in a black shirt with a vibrant orange-and-yellow silk
scarf tied around her neck, looking off to the side against a gray
background.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261027-cleta-mitchell-portrait-redux.jpg?w=752)Cleta
Mitchell founded a grassroots organization, the Election Integrity Network,
devoted to rewriting election laws and rules to be more restrictive. Travis
Dove/The New York Times/Redux

### “Opposed to Honest Elections”

Obtained by ProPublica

No one besides Trump himself has done more than Mitchell, 76, to turn the
mundane processes of how ballots are cast and counted in American elections
into mortal combat.

Since Trump returned to the White House, Mitchell and her acolytes have been
deeply entwined in his unprecedented bid to assert federal control over
voting, an effort that has increasingly defined his second term.

Friends and enemies alike credit her with providing much of the
administration’s election road map. The White House has turned to those close
to her to enact the plan, appointing her associates to help lead the hunt for
noncitizens on voter rolls and to reinvestigate 2020 voting irregularities.

“She has the president’s ear,” Steve Bannon, Trump’s former chief strategist
and a close ally of Mitchell’s, said in a July interview. “A lot of the
momentum things we’ve seen over the last six months or so come directly from
Cleta’s involvement.”

To understand how Mitchell became the hand behind this transformational push,
ProPublica traced her obsession with politics and elections back to its roots.

From the start, those who knew her told us, she stood out for her willingness
to embrace options others wouldn’t and to do whatever it took to win.

Her relentlessness and long-term strategic vision have enabled her to outflank
or outlast not only her liberal opponents, but her conservative rivals.

Much of Mitchell’s influence derives from years of groundwork she’s done to
put a foundation under the so-called election-integrity movement, once
dismissed as a collection of oddballs and fringe actors.

Beyond building the EIN and raising millions of dollars to fund its
activities, she’s helped direct tens of millions more to like-minded policy
shops, researchers, law firms and advocacy groups.

The net effect has been to make an agreed-upon set of beliefs about elections
— that the 2020 presidential vote was stolen, that U.S. voting systems are
rigged, that there’s rampant voting by noncitizens — a core part of
conservatism.

Rick Wilson, a former Republican strategist who collaborated with Mitchell
before Trump’s election and now heads the anti-Trump Lincoln Project, said she
had been crucial in building the institutional infrastructure that has
sustained Trump’s “big lie.”

“What she found in Trump was less of a client and more of a movement,” he
said.

Mitchell declined multiple requests to speak with ProPublica for this article
but occasionally answered emails. “Hahahaha!!!” she wrote in response to one
email asking for an interview. To another, she replied: “You’re my opponent. …
You’re never going to write in any objective, non-judgmental way about the
election integrity movement.”

She responded in writing to about a quarter of our detailed questions,
disputing that her efforts were designed to undermine elections or upend their
results.

“Nothing that we do is designed or intended to ‘sway’ any election outcomes,”
she wrote. “What we focus on is making sure the election process is accurate,
transparent, and honest. The ONLY steps I’ve urged the Administration to take
are those that will give the voters — ALL voters — confidence that the
outcomes are correct.”

A White House spokesperson didn’t answer specific questions about Mitchell,
saying she has no official role in election policy but is an effective private
advocate.

To tell Mitchell’s story, ProPublica interviewed more than 35 people who have
worked with her or know her personally, including participants in her network,
Republican election lawyers, current and former Trump administration
officials, family members and friends. Many, especially conservatives who’ve
fallen out with her, spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared
retribution.

We examined thousands of emails related to her work obtained from public
records requests and sources, as well as court filings and an oral history she
gave in 2007.

We also reviewed hundreds of hours of recordings of her network’s organizing
calls spanning a four-year period, many of which were shared exclusively with
ProPublica, as well as numerous speeches she’s given at private events for
conservatives.

On a call earlier this year, she emphasized that Democrats “only win when they
cheat” and that people who resist EIN’s agenda are “opposed to honest
elections” and “depraved.”

As much as Mitchell has been able to achieve with Trump in the White House,
several people we spoke with noted she hasn’t been able to push important
parts of her agenda over the finish line.

Her signature legislation — the SAVE Act and its successor, the SAVE America
Act — have been blocked by moderate Republicans in the Senate. Election
changes she’d hoped the president could push through before the midterms, such
as compelling states to turn over confidential voter information to the
Justice Department, have been blocked by the courts. And Trump’s mid-July
address on elections drew shrugs even from some conservative media.

Critics, including some inside the election-integrity movement, told
ProPublica they are worried that Mitchell’s growing frustration is prompting
her to press Trump and his allies toward ever more extreme actions. Her
lifelong pattern, ProPublica’s reporting shows, has been to escalate conflicts
into winner-take-all battles — a pattern playing out now as she tries to shape
the midterms.

Hours after Trump’s speech, Mitchell appeared on Bannon’s “War Room” podcast,
sounding openly exasperated at the dismissive coverage, her lips pressed into
a thin line.

Bannon suggested the evidence of election fraud cited by the president
justified declaring a national emergency, which he argued would enable Trump
to immediately force states to implement parts of the SAVE America Act.

Mitchell went even further, one-upping the right-wing provocateur. Trump
needn’t bother with this step, she said, which would inevitably be met with
court challenges. He already had authority under a law empowering the
government to protect critical infrastructure to unilaterally enforce the
bill’s requirements, she insisted.

“We’ve got the blueprint. We’ll help,” she said. “We just need someone in
authority to say, ‘Let’s do it.’”

![A black-and-white photograph shows a young woman smiling while wearing round
glasses, a blazer, a white blouse with a large bow and a ribbon pinned to her
lapel.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261027-cleta-
mitchell-archive.jpg?w=752)Mitchell in 1978 speaking at a gathering for the
Equal Rights Amendment, the proposed constitutional change to guarantee women
the same legal rights as men. The ERA, her signature issue, failed to pass in
her home state of Oklahoma and nationally. Oscar Abolafia/TPLP/Getty Images

### “I Was Always Interested in Politics”

Via Oklahoma State University Library

Mitchell’s fascination with politics and voting began at an early age.

One of her first memories, she would [recount in the 2007 oral
history](https://dc.library.okstate.edu/digital/collection/legislature/id/109),
was begging her mother “please not to go vote” until she got home from school
and could accompany her. Later, she recalled, “I would study all the voter
guides and tell my mother who I thought she ought to vote for.”

Mitchell grew up poor in Oklahoma City, the third of six children born to Jack
Deatherage and Modean Lane. She’s often credited her mother, a secretary, for
pushing her relentlessly to excel. About her father, she’s said much less,
[telling The Wall Street
Journal](https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424127887323844804578528193656378164)
only that he was “kind of a no-account.”

According to court records, their home life was highly volatile. Her mother
[initiated divorce
proceedings](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28829591-d-41047/) at
least five times, citing her father’s [chronic unemployment, drinking, cruelty
and violence](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28829592-d-104815/). The
couple split up for good in 1962, when Cleta was 11.

She hid the family’s struggles behind a peppy disposition, piling up accolades
at school. At 15, she was runner-up in the Oklahoma City Junior Miss pageant.
(Asked about these events, Mitchell replied: “I am peppy. I was also named
Miss Congeniality in that pageant.”)

At the University of Oklahoma, which she attended on a journalism scholarship,
Cleta was known as a “good girl, sorority girl, untouched by the sexual
revolution,” one contemporary said.

Before long, she found a seemingly perfect consort: Duane Draper, who’d been
the university’s student body president. While friends believed their shared
interest in politics brought them together, they had another bond: He, too,
had grown up with an abusive father.

“They were mirror images,” said Conrad Draper, Duane’s brother. “They both
felt powerless in their childhood, so in their adulthood they constantly
pursued power.”

They married in 1971, when Cleta was a junior. When she ran to be student body
president, he served as her unofficial campaign manager.

She lost, a setback she blamed mostly on misogyny. Still, she emerged as
ambitious as ever. She spearheaded voter drives to defeat Republicans, worked
to expand students’ access to voting and helped launch the Oklahoma chapter of
the National Women’s Political Caucus. She served as a delegate at the 1972
Democratic National Convention.

As soon as she graduated from law school, Cleta ran for a seat in the Oklahoma
House of Representatives, taking on an incumbent Republican. She knocked on
every door in her district, prospecting for votes at bowling alleys, beauty
shops and high school football games. When she won, Duane had the campaigning
shoes she’d worn to near-shreds bronzed.

At 26, she joined a Legislature that was literally smoke-filled (it hadn’t
banned cigars) and full of men uneasy at the arrival of “this young, pretty,
opinionated blond,” she said in the oral history. She was undaunted, swiftly
moving up the ranks by cultivating wealthy donors and building a fundraising
machine.

Less than two years later, when Cal Hobson, a small-town mayor contemplating a
House run, asked whose backing he should seek, he was sent to Cleta. She had
only one question when he sought her endorsement, he recalled: Did he back the
[Equal Rights
Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Rights_Amendment), the proposed
constitutional change to guarantee women the same legal rights as men? Hobson
said yes and became her ally in the Legislature, watching as she made “some
friends and a lot of enemies.”

With Democrats in control of the Oklahoma House, she exploited a battle
between candidates for speaker to win a top post on the powerful
Appropriations and Budget Committee, then became its chair.

Once in leadership, she backed a slate of liberal initiatives, from expanding
open records laws to creating training centers to help divorced women improve
their career prospects.

But her idealism coexisted with a ruthless pragmatism, said David Walters, who
came up in Democratic politics in the same era and would eventually become the
state’s governor. He remembered his shock when she promised him she’d oppose a
powerful state development official in a battle over a new building on the
University of Oklahoma campus, then switched sides behind the scenes.

“It was quite remarkable,” Walters said. “This was an example of Cleta saying
one thing publicly and doing in private something entirely different.”

In 1982, with her political fortunes on the rise, Cleta’s marriage to Duane
ended. The filings offered little explanation, citing only “incompatibility,”
but those close to her knew Duane had come out as gay. The heartbreak was
“devastating,” Hobson said.

Duane left Oklahoma for Boston, where he became a gay-rights activist. He died
of AIDS in 1991.

After the divorce, Cleta did what she’d always done: She “put her nose to the
grindstone,” Hobson said, “writing the budget and getting her way at the
Capitol.”

She found a new partner in Dale Mitchell, a former college baseball player,
registered Republican and bank executive. In 1984, when they married, they
agreed that Dale would change his party affiliation if Cleta would take his
last name.

Later that year, [Time magazine named the newly minted Cleta
Mitchell](https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,951140-4,00.html)
as one of a group of star Democratic state legislators, all female, who might
one day “set their sights on a higher prize: the presidency itself.” About a
year after they got married, they welcomed a baby girl.

Then, over two years, their life collapsed.

Her political fortunes waned after the ERA, her signature issue, failed to
pass in Oklahoma and nationally. Her main political patron, the speaker of the
House, had become entangled in a voting-fraud scandal, costing her her
position in leadership. She chose not to defend her House seat, then two years
later ran for lieutenant governor. When she lost, she found herself out of
office completely.

Dale’s troubles dwarfed hers. When oil prices sank, [his overleveraged bank
collapsed](https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/business/1986/08/24/trail-
of-failed-institutions-dog-disillusioned-oklahoma-banker/f34b0ac8-4885-4dbb-
bf32-916119d4d99f/) and federal regulators shut it down. He was banned from
the banking industry and later convicted on multiple counts of bank fraud, for
which he was put on five years’ probation and ordered to pay $3 million in
restitution. The crisis ruined them financially.

Cleta emerged from the ordeal infuriated by what she viewed as federal
government’s overreach in prosecuting her husband, whom she has
[defended](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/1996/10/21/the-outsider-9) as
“the most honest person I’ve ever known.”

Once out of Democratic politics, Mitchell gravitated toward conservatives, who
were gaining ground in much of the country. She explained the shift as a way
to realign her politics to match her personal philosophy of self-sufficiency
(and no government handouts). Others say she saw a route back to power and
took it.

Hobson, who rose to lead Oklahoma’s senate, was gobsmacked by her
transformation.

“No one,” he said, “has changed more politically in my lifetime than Cleta
Deatherage Mitchell.”

![A woman wearing glasses, a white dress and a sash that reads, in part,
“vote” speaks into a microphone at a podium bearing the seal of the president
of the United States, while President Donald Trump watches from off to the
side in a suit and blue tie.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261027-cleta-mitchell-trump.jpg?w=752)Mitchell and
President Donald Trump in August 2020 at an event marking the 100th
anniversary of the ratification of the 19th amendment, which gave women the
right to vote. Mitchell, once involved in Democratic politics, switched her
party affiliation to the Republicans in 1996. Tia Dufour/White House/Planet
Pix via ZUMA Wire/Reuters

### "Consigliere to the Vast Right-Wing Conspiracy"

Hillsdale College, via YouTube

Starting in the early 1990s, Mitchell embarked upon a three-and-a-half decade
climb up the conservative power ladder.

She and Dale moved to Washington, D.C., so she could help lead a mostly
Republican campaign for congressional term limits. Though ultimately
unsuccessful, the fight endeared Mitchell, brought in as the token Democrat,
to the conservative elite. She switched her party affiliation in 1996 and,
within the next few years, had recovered enough financially to buy a home in
an upscale gated community and a luxury vacation getaway in the U.S. Virgin
Islands.

After the 2000 election, as George W. Bush fought to hold onto a narrow lead
over Al Gore in Florida, Mitchell became one of the Bush campaign’s high-
profile media surrogates and defenders. In TV appearances, she argued that
Democrats’ demands for recounts were an attempt to manipulate the election
system.

She emerged determined to focus more of her legal practice on countering what
she saw as an assault by progressive groups on election integrity. If
“Republicans don’t commit themselves to learning and practicing the art of
political war,” she wrote in [a Wall Street Journal
column](https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB974676309640007539), “there may not be
much of a GOP to kick around anymore in the future.”

Over the next eight years, she became a go-to election lawyer for Republican
politicians and [a partner at a powerful D.C. law
firm](https://docs.house.gov/meetings/GO/GO00/20140730/102571/HHRG-113-GO00-Bio-
MitchellC-20140730.pdf). Later, [when the Tea Party
emerged](https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052702304316404575580670676270344),
Mitchell embraced hard-right candidates and causes that some other GOP
attorneys would not.

She jokingly described herself as the “[consigliere to the vast right-wing
conspiracy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bNsLCGdcj5o)” — a [title
others](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3l2lQa0RZhw) found increasingly on the
mark.

As an attorney, Mitchell didn’t particularly shine in the courtroom, those who
worked with her said, but she was a masterful and aggressive backroom
negotiator and strategist.

No longer a candidate herself, she was free not to be “Miss Congeniality,” she
acknowledged in a mentorship speech to conservative women titled “[It’s Better
to Be Respected Than Liked](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGfFGZdoEBA).” She
won over allies with Southern warmth but could be a dangerous enemy if
crossed. She’d do anything — within the law — to win, a dynamic one fellow
election lawyer called “part of her brand.” (Mitchell didn’t respond to the
questions about these assessments.)

Mitchell was one of the first Republican lawyers to support Trump’s
presidential ambitions.

Starting in 2011, [she
defended](https://www.fec.gov/files/legal/murs/6462/13044334588.pdf) him
against a [Federal Election Commission
complaint](https://www.fec.gov/files/legal/murs/6462/13044334588.pdf) that a
website floating a possible Trump run constituted an undeclared candidacy.

Michael Cohen, Trump’s fixer, who helped launch the exploratory bid, said
Mitchell had come recommended as the most aggressive lawyer in the field and
first met the future president when she came to Trump Tower to discuss the
case. Cohen said Trump subsequently retained Mitchell several more times.

“Each matter was [resolved to our
benefit](https://www.fec.gov/files/legal/murs/6462/13044334710.pdf), something
both Trump and I appreciated,” Cohen said in a brief phone interview. When
ProPublica asked what the other matters were, Cohen responded, “I can’t
disclose those,” then hung up.

When Trump ran for real in 2016, Mitchell transferred her support to him once
he’d knocked out her longtime client Marco Rubio. Some of her allies were
shocked she’d back an insurgent candidate who often chafed at constitutional
limits on executive power and violated conservative principles she’d long
espoused.

During Trump’s first term, Reuters reported, Mitchell [teamed with other
prominent GOP lawyers](https://www.reuters.com/world/special-report-how-small-
group-us-lawyers-pushed-voter-fraud-fears-into-2020-09-09/) on efforts to
tighten election laws and rules, focusing on those related to mail-in voting
and voter ID. Mitchell helped steer millions of dollars into these
initiatives, as well as backing lawsuits against Democratic-leaning cities and
counties aimed at compelling them to purge voters from their rolls.

In the run-up to the 2020 election, Mitchell was among the first GOP lawyers
to urge the Trump campaign to develop plans to dispute the contest’s results,
focusing on six to eight battleground states.

Mitchell’s subsequent role in helping Trump try to challenge his loss has been
much chronicled in news articles and examined in [multiple
investigations](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-J6-TRANSCRIPT-
CTRL0000083769/pdf/GPO-J6-TRANSCRIPT-CTRL0000083769.pdf). Over time, experts
said, it’s become clear she helped originate several of the most aggressive
actions taken by the president and his allies.

![A large crowd of rioters fights with police officers wearing helmets and
face shields inside the rotunda of the U.S. Capitol. Historic paintings line
the curved stone walls in the background.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261027-cleta-mitchell-jan6.jpg?w=752)Police and
rioters clash during the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Mostafa
Bassim/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images

“She had her finger in just about every pie the select committee looked at,”
said Marc Harris, senior investigative counsel to the House [congressional
committee that investigated](https://www.govinfo.gov/collection/january-6th-
committee-final-
report?path=/GPO/January%206th%20Committee%20Final%20Report%20and%20Supporting%20Materials%20Collection)
the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the capitol.

Mitchell led litigation on the president’s behalf in Georgia, accumulating
[1,800 pages of election fraud
allegations](https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/Pak%20Ex%205%20-%20SJC-
Pre-CertificationEvents-000598-6651.pdf). She maintains events moved too fast
for this material to be properly evaluated by a judge. “President Trump NEVER
got his day in court in GA,” she wrote in response to ProPublica’s questions.

These claims figured prominently in the [infamous phone
call](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/trump-raffensperger-call-
georgia-vote/2021/01/03/d45acb92-4dc4-11eb-bda4-615aaefd0555_story.html) on
which she joined Trump as he pressed Georgia Secretary of State Brad
Raffensperger to “find” him enough votes to overcome Biden’s slim margin in
the state.

As Trump poured on the pressure, Mitchell fed him details of election
irregularities from her case and demanded that Raffensperger share his
findings from investigations into them.

Mitchell insisted to ProPublica they merely wanted to provide Raffensperger
with evidence, not to push him “to take any official action to ‘overturn the
election.’”

In the call, Trump made [clear what he
wanted](https://www.cnn.com/2021/01/03/politics/trump-brad-raffensperger-
phone-call-transcript).

“All we have to do, Cleta, is find 11,000-plus votes,” he said.

Mitchell also played a largely overlooked role in launching Trump’s final and
most extreme gambit, the so-called fake electors strategy.

She [recruited](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-J6-TRANSCRIPT-
CTRL0000083769/pdf/GPO-J6-TRANSCRIPT-CTRL0000083769.pdf) her longtime friend,
[law professor John
Eastman](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-J6-TRANSCRIPT-
CTRL0000083769/pdf/GPO-J6-TRANSCRIPT-CTRL0000083769.pdf), to prepare a memo
[outlining a constitutional framework](https://americanmind.org/memo/the-
constitutional-authority-of-state-legislatures-to-choose-electors/) under
which Republican legislators in swing states where Trump had lost could
appoint alternate electors who’d support him.

In her emailed responses to ProPublica, Mitchell called the idea an outgrowth
of work she’d done early that year advising the [American Legislative Exchange
Council](https://alec.org/article/exploring-alecs-essential-policy-solutions-
for-2025/) about steps state lawmakers could take to help Trump in a contested
election.

“A movement is stirring,” Mitchell [wrote to Eastman in an
email](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cacd.841840/gov.uscourts.cacd.841840.350.10.pdf)
two days after the election released by the House Jan. 6 Committee. “But needs
constitutional support.”

Ultimately, what congressional investigators came to call the [“Trump-Eastman
scheme”](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-J6-REPORT/html-
submitted/ch5.html) culminated with a plan for Vice President Mike Pence to
certify the fake electors’ votes, flipping the Electoral College in Trump’s
favor. But Pence rejected the idea, becoming the target of enraged Trump
supporters when they stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6.

Experts said Mitchell helped set the day’s events in motion though she was not
at the riot.

“She worked closely with John Eastman in developing and seeking to implement
dubious legal strategies to overturn the election result,” Harris said. “She
encouraged the selection of fake electors.”

Mitchell denied any responsibility for Eastman’s work or what ensued.

“I was completely uninvolved in the Jan 6 rally at the Capitol,” she wrote in
response to ProPublica’s questions. “I had nothing to do with the issues and
advice from Dr. Eastman to the President, the Vice-President, or anyone else
involved in that. None whatsoever.”

In an email responding to ProPublica’s questions, Eastman acknowledged
Mitchell had solicited the memo but disputed his strategy was aimed at
upending the election.

The California Supreme Court [disbarred Eastman for his
actions](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/news/attorney-john-eastman-disbarred-
california-supreme-court).

Mitchell resigned from her law firm after the Raffensperger call sparked
backlash, blaming her exit on pressure from anti-Trump groups.

But unlike many who’d fought alongside her, Mitchell wasn’t dispirited once
Biden entered the White House. She was just getting started.

![A woman gestures from behind a wooden lectern as she speaks into a
microphone. She is standing beside a South Carolina state flag with a
presentation slide titled “SIGNIFICANT FACTS ABOUT 2020” projected behind
her.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261027-cleta-
mitchell-slideshow.jpg?w=752)Mitchell speaks about election integrity at a
South Carolina Republican Party conference in Myrtle Beach. Gerard Albert
III/Myrtle Beach Sun News/Tribune News Service via Getty Images

### “Hand-to-Hand Combat With the Left, Starting at the Local Level”

Obtained by ProPublica

In 2022, behind the closed doors of hotel ballrooms and conference suites,
Mitchell appealed to crowds of conservatives in seven swing states, asking
them to help her overhaul U.S. elections.

“Welcome, fellow deplorables!” she said to open the proceedings in Michigan,
after a welcome video from Trump urging the crowd to get behind her. “As an
old Southern Baptist, I like evangelizing. So, this is your Bible!”

Brandishing the [20-page
manual](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/22189074-conservative-
partnership-institute-and-election-integrity-network-citizens-guide/) provided
to each participant, Mitchell implored attendees to master the arcane rules of
American elections, work the polls and cozy up to — or, better yet, serve on —
local election boards.

The tour was part of the nationwide launch of the Election Integrity Network.
In the aftermath of losing the fight over 2020, Mitchell decided she needed an
army — a popular movement large and loud enough to tear down what she saw as
an election system dominated by Democrats.

“My sole focus has been for the last year and a half, how we as conservatives
could build an infrastructure to do hand-to-hand combat with the Left,
starting at the local level,” she said on a September 2022 EIN organizing
call.

The network served as the centerpiece, providing the boots on the ground, but
Mitchell also created an ecosystem to support it, spreading money to allied
researchers, law firms and policy shops.

A ProPublica analysis of data from the Campaign Legal Center, a government
watchdog nonprofit, shows that between 2021 and 2025, Mitchell helped put more
than $70 million into this work. According to tax filings, at least $11
million of that total came from nonprofits she oversaw. Tens of millions more
came from the Bradley Foundation, where she served on the board, and the
[Conservative Partnership Institute](https://cpi.org/staff/cleta-mitchell/), a
Trump-aligned think tank where she was a senior legal fellow.

Roughly 30 conservative election-integrity nonprofits were started after 2020.
Well over half have received money from Mitchell or have close ties with her,
the data shows.

“She occupies a unique position,” connecting donors, activists and political
leaders, said Brendan Fischer, the Campaign Legal Center’s director of
strategic investigations. She’s leveraged this spot, he said, “to turn
election denial from a fringe position into an organized national movement.”

In assembling the EIN, Mitchell built chapters from scratch in some states; in
others, she absorbed long-standing groups that did similar work.

Much of the network’s organizing takes place on the regular video calls held
by each state chapter and about half a dozen national working groups, which
focus on subjects such as reshaping voter rolls and scrutinizing voting
machines.

In reviewing hundreds of hours of these meetings, ProPublica found a mixture
of mind-numbing technical discussions, wild speculation and hyperpartisan
vitriol.

On a July 2025 call to honor Eastman, he urged network leaders to assault the
Left as the Romans attacked the ancient city of
[Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Carthage_\(Third_Punic_War\)).
“They will never stop until not only are they defeated, but the land from
which they came is salted over so they can’t grow up again,” he said.

Mitchell disputed that EIN was partisan. “I defy you to show me hyperpartisan
vitriol on any EIN related call,” she wrote to ProPublica. “That is not what
we do. Mind-numbing technical discussions, yes.”

Local calls often fixate on micro-efforts aimed at a single county or election
office. Members — who sometimes call themselves “election believers,” a
counter to the “election denier” label used by critics — discuss lobbying
particular politicians or combing voting records for evidence of fraud. If, as
often happens, they find no widespread problems, the meetings serve as echo
chambers in which supporters are urged to keep the faith and see conspiracies
behind small bureaucratic mistakes.

Current and former members said being in the network made them feel like part
of a special strike force saving America. Mitchell’s charm could be
irresistible.

“It’s like she’s the sun and you’re the sunflower,” a former EIN leader said,
speaking on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation. But Mitchell’s
wrath could be volcanic if members disagreed with her or explored working with
other election-integrity groups.

“Vindictive is not a strong enough word,” the former EIN leader said. “She
treats you like a heretic.”

(Mitchell didn’t respond to these observations.)

Mitchell joins rank-and-file calls every month or so, on which she’s praised
effusively and given titles like “the world’s leading expert on election
integrity” and “our patron saint.” She also chairs a Friday morning leadership
meeting that draws high-profile guests like Lisa Nelson, the head of the
American Legislative Exchange Council, state election officials and luminaries
from conservative think tanks. “It’s a who’s-who of who matters in the
movement,” the former member said.

Since Trump retook the White House, officials from his administration have
occasionally attended, discussing how they can coordinate with the network’s
activists.

In summer 2025, a DHS official joined a network call to discuss an effort to
persuade states to use an agency tool to search their voter rolls for
noncitizens. Many [states had
resisted](https://www.propublica.org/article/save-voter-citizenship-tool-
mistakes-confusion), uneasy about sharing confidential data with the federal
government. The official wanted network members to encourage state and local
officials to cooperate.

“This is your team,” an EIN leader said. “These are the people that are going
to do the work in the states that you need to make this magic happen.”

Early on, many EIN branches weren’t particularly effective and several had
notable stumbles. A then-participant in North Carolina’s chapter [accompanied
a group that unsuccessfully tried](https://www.propublica.org/article/north-
carolina-election-denial-voting-surry) to force its way into a voting office.
The chapter’s leader was accused of [following election
workers](https://rantnc.com/2022/05/16/womack-asks-again-for-access-to-voting-
machines-follows-vehicle-bringing-early-ballots-to-elections-office/) in his
car and other disruptive behavior. (He denied his actions were problematic.)

But by 2023, the network started getting significant wins.

Mitchell and EIN were instrumental in spurring Republican states to pull out
of a [program to cross-check voter
rolls](https://www.npr.org/2023/06/04/1171159008/eric-investigation-voter-
data-election-integrity) for duplicate registrations. Mitchell claimed the
program aided Democrats by requiring states to encourage unregistered
residents to sign up to vote.

EIN members also helped persuade [numerous states to pass
laws](https://www.governing.com/finance/28-states-have-banned-or-restricted-
private-funds-for-elections) banning “Zuckerbucks” — private donations from
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and others aimed at bolstering underfunded local
election offices. Mitchell had claimed the donations helped Democratic
turnout, paying for things like Spanish translators in election offices.

EIN continued to grow, expanding from seven chapters in 2022 to at least 26
today.

In Georgia, the network came close to realizing the goals Mitchell sketched
out when she first pitched the group.

EIN members secretly [pushed a rule through the State Election
Board](https://www.propublica.org/article/georgia-election-board-vote-
certification) allowing local officials to delay certifying the state’s vote
count — a step [experts warned could enable them to dispute a Trump
loss](https://www.propublica.org/article/georgia-election-rule-could-exclude-
votes) in the upcoming 2024 election. (Mitchell disputed that the rule change
was aimed at this.)

A [court struck down the rule](https://www.propublica.org/article/georgia-
election-results-certification-counting-votes), but that didn’t stop a group
aligned with Mitchell from [mounting an ad campaign
urging](https://www.propublica.org/article/2024-election-certification-ads-
georgia-wisconsin-pennsylvania) election officials nationwide not to certify
results they didn’t like.

As her state-level plans advanced, Mitchell readied an even bigger swing, one
aimed at changing elections across the country and setting the agenda for a
second Trump administration.

### “God Made Me Do This”

Obtained by ProPublica

In January 2024, Mitchell met with a small group of Republican lawyers and
election-integrity leaders to discuss how best to prevent fraud in the
November presidential election.

Those gathered in the Arizona hotel room were especially worried about
noncitizen voting, though numerous [audits, studies and
analyses](https://fairelectionscenter.org/voting-by-noncitizens-is-a-non-
issue/) — even those [by Republican groups and
states](https://www.cato.org/commentary/trumps-claims-about-noncitizens-
voting-are-false-we-can-prove-it) — show it [is vanishingly
rare](https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-
voting-missing-millions).

Arizona had passed a law compelling residents to provide proof of citizenship
when they registered, rather than just swearing they were citizens under
penalty of perjury, as is typical in most states.

Mitchell suddenly had an inspiration, she later recounted in a private speech
to Virginia’s EIN chapter: She’d lead a push for a similar federal law. “I
didn’t think of this,” she told those at the event. “God made me do this.”

When Mitchell returned from Arizona, she was, indeed, a woman on a mission.
She convened her closest congressional allies, Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and Rep.
Chip Roy of Texas. Their staffers met with her to help draft the [Safeguard
American Voter Eligibility
Act](https://www.lee.senate.gov/services/files/0BAFB7AD-0DFA-4C00-8C98-CAC6C4F35FD8).

The bill set a high bar for proving citizenship, demanding that would-be
voters produce documents like certified birth certificates and passports that
many Americans don’t have. It also required states to use the DHS’ databases
to purge noncitizens from their voter rolls.

The ideas in the measure would presage some of the second Trump
administration’s most norm-breaking actions. “When we look back to the
original SAVE Act in 2024 to the administration’s actions today, the through
line is clear,” said Michael McNulty, a director for the watchdog nonprofit
Issue One.

Mitchell knew the initial version of the act wouldn’t pass. When it was
introduced in May 2024, Democrats controlled the Senate and the White House.

Rather, people in the election-integrity world said, she saw the measure as a
strategic opportunity — both to cement her position atop the movement and to
reignite the fervor for voting restrictions among the Trump faithful. For
years, she’d fought behind the scenes for Trump’s ear on election issues,
vying with more moderate Republican election experts as well as fringe
activists.

To make sure her rivals had no choice but to support the SAVE Act, she brought
on a backer too powerful to ignore: Stephen Miller, senior adviser to Trump in
his first term and architect of his immigration policy. (Miller didn’t respond
to questions about his relationship to Mitchell or the SAVE Act.)

Mitchell denied Miller had a hand in the measure. “Stephen is someone I
greatly admire but we never worked together on the SAVE Act,” she wrote to
ProPublica.

![A man stands outdoors in a gray plaid suit and tie, positioned between a man
wearing sunglasses on the left and a smiling Cleta Mitchell on the
right.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261027-cleta-
mitchell-stephen-miller.jpg?w=752)Stephen Miller, center, senior adviser to
Trump in his first term and architect of his immigration policy, attends the
May 2024 news conference for the SAVE Act. Kent Nishimura/Getty Images

But Roy, the bill’s House sponsor, said [in a podcast
interview](https://www.mediamatters.org/justice-civil-liberties/rep-chip-roy-
says-election-deniers-and-project-2025-contributors-helped) that Miller helped
draft it. Mitchell sought to dovetail her election agenda with Miller’s
immigration agenda, those who’ve worked with them said. They stood side by
side at an event at the Capitol to launch the bill, warning that Democrats
were letting people into the country illegally in part to swing elections.

In a coup for Mitchell — anointed the [Mother of the SAVE
Act](https://www.realclearpolitics.com/articles/2026/09/18/the_mother_of_the_save_act_154513.html)
— pretty much every significant player in the election-integrity space joined
the [Only Citizens Vote Coalition](https://www.onlycitizensvotecoalition.com),
a group she launched to back the bill.

Mitchell directed more than $6 million to groups that bought ads, put out
research and took other actions supporting SAVE, tax filings show. Some
$800,000 went to the nonprofit arm of the conservative media organization The
Federalist, which provided glowing coverage of the legislation.

Sean Davis, The Federalist’s CEO, didn’t answer questions about whether the
donation affected coverage. “Cleta Mitchell is a saint,” he said in an email.

The measure [sailed through the House](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-
congress/house-bill/8281) in July 2024, then predictably died in the Senate.
The bill had drawn fire from [voting advocacy
groups](https://my.lwv.org/missouri/metro-st-louis/article/save-act-would-
disenfranchise-many-voters), which said the measure could disenfranchise
[millions of eligible voters](https://www.americanprogress.org/article/the-
save-act-would-disenfranchise-millions-of-citizens/), particularly women, the
poor and minorities, all critical Democratic voting blocs.

Mitchell hardly missed a beat. That same month, she led a panel at an
[American Legislative Exchange Council
conference](https://www.exposedbycmd.org/featured-documents/cleta-mitchell-
email-lobbying-alec-lawmakers-to-pass-only-citizens-vote-model-
policy-7-17-24/) that approved model legislation similar to the SAVE Act for
[conservative lawmakers to introduce in states across the
country](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/article/2024/aug/23/non-citizen-
voting-alec-bill). [Twelve states have since passed
laws](https://www.americanprogress.org/article/the-save-act-may-be-stalled-in-
congress-but-state-versions-are-being-advanced-all-across-the-country/) that
strongly resembled SAVE and 23 have [changed their voting procedures to
reflect aspects](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/trumps-voting-
restrictions-bill-may-fail-parts-live-23-states-2026-04-14/) of it.

That November, Trump won back the presidency and Republicans secured
majorities in both chambers of Congress.

Mitchell saw the chance not only to pass an even tougher federal version of
SAVE — a “SAVE Act on steroids” as she called it in a November organizing call
— but to make even more far-reaching changes to American elections.

“This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity,” she told attendees on the call.
“I don’t want us to miss this.”

Donald Trump in March 2025. When Trump won back the presidency and Republicans

### “If Plan A Doesn’t Work, I Have a Plan B”

Obtained by ProPublica

Two months after Trump took the oath of office, America got its first glimpse
of how he planned to overhaul the nation’s election system.

His March 25, 2025, executive order — titled [Preserving and Protecting the
Integrity of American Elections](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-
actions/2025/03/preserving-and-protecting-the-integrity-of-american-
elections/) — looked a lot like the SAVE Act. It required voters to prove
their citizenship when they registered, mirroring the types of identification
listed in the bill.

It also expanded on the notion of using DHS data to verify voters’
eligibility, saying that all of the federal government’s relevant troves of
sensitive information should be made available for this use. Further, it
directed the Justice Department to prioritize the prosecution of election
crimes and noncitizen voting.

Mitchell was close to a pair of White House lawyers involved in drafting the
order and was among a small group of outside attorneys who provided
suggestions for it, according to several people who helped write it.

The order was the first in a string of behind-the-scenes victories that have
not only allowed Mitchell to shape the Trump administration’s election
blueprint, but have given her substantial influence over who’s been chosen to
carry it out.

At least 25 administration appointees have close ties to Mitchell,
ProPublica’s reporting shows, with several holding key posts directly related
to elections.

“She’s had a lot to do with even White House hires in this regard,” Bannon
said. (The White House denied Mitchell had swayed its hiring decisions.)

Heather Honey, a senior counselor to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne
Mullin, has a portfolio that touches on almost everything the administration
does on elections. She’s figured centrally in the government’s efforts to find
and prosecute noncitizen voters.

Before joining DHS, Honey was a Mitchell protege and led EIN’s Pennsylvania
chapter. A high-ranking federal official knowledgeable about the hiring
process told ProPublica that the agency hired Honey over more experienced
candidates. Her “sole qualification was who she worked with,” the former
official said. “She worked with Cleta.”

A DHS spokesperson called this “false,” saying Honey had been recommended by
senior government leaders for her election expertise.

Mitchell also has had a hand in shaping the administration’s reinvestigation
of fraud allegations involving the 2020 election, beginning with the FBI’s
[seizure of election records](https://www.propublica.org/article/fbi-fulton-
county-voting-records-search-warrant) from Fulton County, Georgia.

As ProPublica has reported, the affidavit justifying the raid included
material [compiled by an EIN-affiliated
researcher](https://www.propublica.org/article/kevin-moncla-election-
researcher-fulton-county-georgia) and cited network participants as witnesses.

When the case bogged down as the prosecutor overseeing it began to doubt its
strength, Mitchell was among those who recommended a replacement: Dan Bishop,
a former North Carolina congressman whom she’s
[praised](https://x.com/CletaMitchell/status/1837662050383696152?s=20) on
[social media](https://x.com/CletaMitchell/status/1837624091844460898?s=20)
and [supported with campaign
donations](https://www.opensecrets.org/search?page=4&q=Cleta+Mitchell&type=donors).

At a May meeting, a Georgia EIN leader said Bishop was tapped “thanks in large
part to Cleta Mitchell,” an account echoed by an administration official
familiar with the matter.

A Justice Department spokesperson said the agency “has no knowledge of any
role Cleta Mitchell played” in Bishop’s appointment.

Mitchell told ProPublica she didn’t believe she’d affected this decision. “I
was very worried about the direction of the case earlier this year and made
known my displeasure quite strongly,” she said. “The decision to appoint Dan
was made by the President and I applaud it, but I cannot claim credit for that
brilliant idea.”

Soon after stepping in, Bishop tried to [subpoena personal
information](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/may/05/fulton-county-
election-workers-us-attorney-subpoena) for thousands of Fulton County poll
workers, a move the county and election experts denounced as politically
motivated intimidation. A court quashed the subpoena. [Bishop has
appealed.](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.ca11.97232/gov.uscourts.ca11.97232.17.0.pdf)

As she’d envisioned in her call with EIN members just after the 2024 election,
Mitchell has gotten the president to sink enormous political capital into
passing [even tougher versions of the
bill](https://www.americanprogress.org/article/the-save-america-act-explained-
how-the-new-show-your-papers-voting-bill-is-even-more-extreme-than-the-save-
act/), now known as the SAVE America Act.

The 2026 measure would require voters nationwide to present photo ID to vote
and compel states to turn over their voter rolls to DHS, which [would scour
them for noncitizens](https://americafirstpolicy.com/issues/the-save-america-
act-strengthening-protections-for-federal-elections/). Trump has repeatedly
called the measure his [top legislative
priority](https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/03/09/congress/trump-
save-america-act-gop-00819673), threatening not to sign other bills until it
passes.

Lee, the Utah senator who [sponsored the
bill](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-
bill/3752/cosponsors), said Mitchell was central to the updated version,
especially the strict voter ID provisions. Trump, he added, gave it the new
name.

Former officials and people in the election-integrity movement told ProPublica
that Mitchell has had to overcome naysayers within the administration,
including White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

On an EIN call in early 2025, Mitchell complained that Wiles had responded
frostily to plans she offered for the incoming administration, “saying, ‘Thank
you, I’ll take a look as soon as I come up for air.’”

At the time, Mitchell said she’d wanted to reply that wouldn’t happen for four
years. When ProPublica followed up about the incident, she wrote: “Susie is
remarkable and a great chief of staff. She doesn’t have time to read all the
things that people like me send her.”

Mitchell has surmounted these obstacles, in part, by continuing to build out
her array of alliances.

By the middle of this year, when the White House brought on Solomon — a
longtime [Mitchell
supporter](https://x.com/Bannons_WarRoom/status/2093093494747197576?s=20) who
vetted material for Trump’s prime-time elections address — it was clear she
had found another way in. (A White House spokesperson said that Solomon, who
also runs a conservative news site, interacted with Mitchell as a journalist
would speak to a subject-matter expert.)

A former administration official who said he’d tried to stymie Mitchell
acknowledged she’d won out. “The White House listens to her,” he said.

Mitchell had told her EIN disciples not to worry after Wiles’ brush off. She
had more cards to play, she assured them.

“I always know if plan A doesn’t work, I have a plan B,” she said. “If plan B
doesn’t work, I have a plan C. And so forth.”

January 2026. “Even if she fails, she always finds another point of attack,”

### “Today”

Steve Bannon’s “War Room” Podcast

By the time the first mail-in ballots of the midterms were cast in September,
Mitchell had shaped and staffed the Trump administration’s election efforts to
an astonishing extent. And yet, the knockout blow had eluded her.

Courts had blocked large parts of Trump’s executive orders. The [hunt for
noncitizen voters](https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-
homeland-security-investigations) and the reinvestigation of 2020 voting
irregularities had produced little of consequence, despite the considerable
resources poured into them.

Mitchell’s critics and even her allies, including some in the election-
integrity movement, say frustration has prompted her to push for more drastic
steps.

During the summer, she mounted an escalating pressure campaign [to save the
SAVE America
Act](https://www.realclearpolitics.com/articles/2026/09/18/the_mother_of_the_save_act_154513.html),
mobilizing EIN members to badger recalcitrant senators, according to
recordings of EIN meetings. She [also worked with the bill’s Senate
sponsor](https://www.realclearpolitics.com/articles/2026/09/18/the_mother_of_the_save_act_154513.html)
and [Trump to kill the
filibuster](https://www.politico.com/news/2025/11/04/trump-senate-republicans-
filibuster-00634517), a pathway known as [the nuclear
option](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_option), to get the bill over
the line, but was blocked by a handful of moderate Republicans.

Mitchell has taken a similarly all-or-nothing approach in pressing states to
pass laws modeled on the SAVE America Act, sometimes with similarly self-
defeating results.

Earlier this year, she waded into a battle over an Ohio bill despite being
warned that the governor would veto the tougher version she preferred. The
final bill contained the provision Mitchell sought. The [governor promptly
vetoed](https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/2026/06/25/ohio-gov-mike-dewine-vetoes-
bill-requiring-mail-in-voters-show-a-copy-of-their-id-to-vote/) it.

Former Ohio Secretary of State Ken Blackwell, [an election-integrity movement
leader](https://americafirstpolicy.com/team/kennethblackwell/) who’s worked
with Mitchell for decades, said Mitchell sometimes runs the risk of making
elections less secure by torpedoing practical solutions.

“It was her way or the highway,” he said. “We need to focus on getting
concrete wins.”

(Mitchell didn’t respond to Blackwell’s broader criticism but called the more
moderate election measure he’s backed in Ohio “not nearly as good as it should
be.”)

As the midterms near, she has become increasingly vocal — in media
appearances, online and with her network members — in calling for the
president to exert unprecedented powers to sway the vote.

“Even if she fails, she always finds another point of attack,” said Max
Flugrath, a director at the voting advocacy group Fair Fight. “She’s
relentless.”

On the [Oct. 6 episode of “War Room,”](https://rumble.com/v7ggxi8-cleta-
mitchell-calls-on-secretary-lutnick-to-implement-dhs-election-
system-.html?e9s=src_v1_cbl%2Csrc_v1_ucp_a) Mitchell angrily pounded home that
several agencies, particularly the Commerce Department, could intervene
“today” to shore up purported vulnerabilities in voting machines. She repeated
the word “today” seven times during the appearance, like a drumbeat.

Some of those who’ve known Mitchell the longest say her urgency has
crescendoed as, at 76, she’s confronted the possibility that this
administration is her last chance to realize her goals.

“In her mind, in her timeline, it’s existential,” the former network leader
said. “She’s got to do it all, and she’s got to do it now. … The election
integrity movement, c’est moi.”
